question:
Patient note:
An 88-year-old woman, a retired elementary school principal who still tutors neighborhood children in arithmetic twice a week, arrived to the internal-medicine clinic this morning for a comprehensive evaluation requested by her ophthalmologist before scheduling elective cataract extraction under monitored anesthesia. She walked from the parking lot without assistance but admitted that she now prefers using the building’s elevators rather than climbing more than one flight, citing limited endurance and a tendency to wheeze in cold air. The breathing limitation is familiar to her: she smoked one pack of cigarettes daily from age 18 until quitting 20 years ago and was told a decade ago, after spirometry performed during an influenza hospitalization, that her airways showed fixed obstruction that only partially improved with bronchodilator. Since that admission she inhales tiotropium 18 µg every morning, fluticasone–salmeterol 250/50 µg one blister twice daily, and keeps an albuterol metered-dose inhaler in her purse, using two puffs before climbing church choir loft stairs or when dusting high shelves; she has avoided emergency-department visits for the last two winters, has never required mechanical ventilation, and her most recent pulmonology note recorded an FEV1 of 1.3 L (56 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 and a diffusing capacity of 60 % predicted. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, leg swelling, or episodes of crushing substernal pain; reviews of prior electrocardiograms reveal normal intervals without pathologic Q waves, and serial cardiac enzyme sets drawn during two separate evaluations for atypical chest discomfort five and seven years ago remained below assay detection. Ten years previously her primary physician discovered fasting plasma glucose readings around 150 mg/dL on two separate mornings; she began metformin 1000 mg twice daily and attended diabetes-education classes at the local senior center. A hemoglobin A1c returned last week measured 7.1 %, and the logbook she carried shows pre-breakfast capillary values from 100 to 160 mg/dL. She endorses intact light-touch sensation in the toes, walks barefoot on carpet without imbalance, passes an annual dilated retinal exam with no hemorrhages or macular changes, and her urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio last month was 18 mg/g. Three years ago mildly elevated aminotransferase values—alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L—prompted abdominal ultrasonography that demonstrated a homogeneous but slightly echogenic liver measuring 15 cm with smooth capsule, patent portal flow, and no splenic enlargement; total bilirubin has remained 0.7–0.9 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1, and she denies jaundice, pruritus, abdominal distention, variceal bleeding, confusion, or easy bruising. She consumes half a glass of sherry on holidays, avoids acetaminophen beyond 1 g per day, and takes no herbal supplements. Her renal indices drawn this morning reveal sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 72 mL/min/1.73 m². Lipid panel shows total cholesterol 184 mg/dL, LDL 96 mg/dL, HDL 52 mg/dL, and triglycerides 132 mg/dL; she takes atorvastatin 20 mg nightly without muscle aches. She never experienced sudden unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, or visual field loss and recounts completing the morning newspaper crossword in ink daily. Her daughter corroborates that household bills are paid on time and notes no personality change, wandering, or short-term memory lapses. Current medications also include aspirin 81 mg daily for vasculoprotection, calcium–vitamin D supplementation, and a nightly 5 mg zolpidem tablet for sleep maintenance; she is allergic to sulfonamide antibiotics, which once produced widespread urticaria. Review of systems is negative for melena, hematemesis, peptic discomfort, joint swelling, photosensitivity rashes, night sweats, weight loss, fevers, hematuria, or flank pain. Vital signs in clinic: temperature 36.5 °C, blood pressure 126/68 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94 % on ambient air at rest, dropping to 91 % after a brisk 30-meter corridor walk, recovering to baseline within one minute. She appears well nourished with a body-mass index of 26 kg/m², speaks in full sentences, and does not use accessory muscles. Conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric, and pupils equal and reactive; oropharynx is clear without thrush. Neck is supple, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and jugular venous pulsation is 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. The point of maximal impulse lies in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung examination discloses diminished breath sounds and scattered end-expiratory wheezes bilaterally with prolonged expiratory phase but no crackles or egophony. Percussion is hyper-resonant symmetrically, diaphragmatic excursion is limited to 3 cm, and tactile fremitus is reduced. Abdomen is flat, soft, with normal bowel tones; percussion yields a liver span of 9 cm, and the edge is smooth, palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, non-tender. There is no shifting dullness or fluid wave. Extremities are warm, radial and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+ bilaterally, no cyanosis, clubbing, or edema, and capillary refill is under two seconds. Neurologic assessment shows an alert, oriented woman with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength in all limbs, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady tandem gait; she completes serial sevens without error. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained today displays normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min, axis within normal limits, no pathologic Q waves, ST-segment deviation, or conduction abnormalities. Portable chest radiograph shows a vertically oriented heart of normal size, flattened diaphragms, and increased retrosternal airspace without focal infiltrates. She seeks counsel on whether her inhaled regimen is adequate for the perioperative period, strategies to keep blood glucose stable while fasting the morning of surgery, and timing of hepatology follow-up given her consistently mild enzyme elevations.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums age points and weighted chronic conditions present at presentation.
- Age 88: the ≥80-year category scores 4 points.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: persistent airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC 0.55) requiring maintenance inhalers scores 1 point.
- Uncomplicated diabetes: treated with metformin, without documented neuropathy, retinopathy, or nephropathy, scores 1 point.
- Mild liver disease: persistent mild aminotransferase elevations and an echogenic liver, with preserved synthetic function and no evidence of portal hypertension, score 1 point.
- No other qualifying comorbidity is documented: 0 points.
Total = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 7.
Final answer: 7
